title: Keep an Engineering Journal
text:
One record per controlled change
Copy this outline into a notebook Markdown cell or a text file beside your project. Do not treat a confident explanation as a substitute for a recorded test.







Field
What to record




Task contract
Input, success, stop condition, budget, permission, forbidden actions


Baseline
The simplest non-agentic solution and the same test inputs


Prediction
Expected output or failure before you run


Run manifest
Code revision, environment, fixture/model configuration, command


Observation
Output, state, tool calls, latency/cost where measured


Failure
Expected versus actual, smallest reproducer, earliest failing boundary


Change
One controlled edit and its rationale


Evaluation
Ordinary, boundary, and adversarial cases; repeated trials where relevant


Decision
Keep, simplify, reject, or investigate; explain the limitation

title: Keep an Engineering Journal
text:
Preserve a useful failure
For the smoke lab, try a one-decision budget. Record that addition executes but a final answer does not: the second decision is forbidden by the limit. Do not rewrite the expected status simply to make a test pass. Contrast this with a normal two-decision run and explain which behavior is part of the runtime contract.

title: Keep an Engineering Journal
text:
Keep the record safe
Use synthetic data. Record concise observable action rationales, not private chain-of-thought. Redact credentials, personal data, authenticated page contents, and sensitive tool payloads. A recorded fixture is redistributed data: check its license and permission before adding it to the repository.

title: Run the Offline Agent Smoke Lab
text:
Level: Project-ready Python
Estimated time: 30–45 minutes
You will check: The package reproduces a known run and enforces a decision budget and tool allowlist.
Practice in: Colab, JupyterLab, or a local editor.
Open this lesson in Google Colab
This is an infrastructure smoke lab, not the complete Unit 0 lesson. It uses a fake model with a fixed decision rule. No language model, provider account, GPU, secret, or inference request is involved. Passing it demonstrates a narrow software contract, not agent intelligence or production readiness.
Three questions guide the check:

title: Run the Offline Agent Smoke Lab
text:
1. Start from a clean environment
In the generated notebook: the first setup cell bundles the course’s Python source. Run it before the examples; it needs no network installation. Restart the kernel and run from the top rather than relying on another notebook’s imports.
Locally: from a checkout, run these commands in a terminal, not a Python cell:
conda env create -f conda.yaml  # First setup only
conda activate fc-agentic
python scripts/check_environment.py
poetry install --extras notebooks
poetry run python -m freecampus_agents.lab
The final command should print a JSON record with status complete, answer 12, and four events. The development installation needs package-registry access once; the smoke run itself does not. See the contributor guide for lockfile status and full development checks.






Warning



Use synthetic data only. This runtime is a teaching example, not a security sandbox. A custom model is trusted in-process Python code; the tool allowlist does not isolate arbitrary code in that model. The future security units address real isolation.

title: Run the Offline Agent Smoke Lab
section: 2. Predict the task, action, observation, and answer
text:
2. Predict the task, action, observation, and answer
Before running, predict the event order and final sum.
from freecampus_agents.lab import Task, run_agent, smoke_test

run = smoke_test()
assert run.status == "complete"
assert run.answer == 12
for event in run.events:
    print(event.kind, event.detail)
Expected output:
task Add 7 and 5
tool_call add
observation 12
final 12
Task stores two integer operands. FakeModel asks for the add tool when there is no observation. run_agent checks the tool name against its allowlist, adds the operands, and records the observation. On the next decision, the fake model returns that observation. The runtime accepts the answer only if it matches the observed integer. smoke_test also compares the whole record with a packaged JSON fixture.
The trace is observable activity, not a private reasoning transcript. Four trace events do not mean four model decisions: this run makes two decisions.

The runtime mediates every requested tool action and checks the final result.





flowchart LR
  T[Task] --> M[Fake model]
  M --> R[Runtime checks]
  R --> A[Addition tool]
  A --> O[Observation]
  O --> M
  R --> F[Final result]

title: Run the Offline Agent Smoke Lab
section: 3. Change one input and check every downstream effect
text:
3. Change one input and check every downstream effect
Predict the new sum, observation, and final event before running:
changed = run_agent(Task(7, 8))
assert changed.answer == 15
assert changed.events[0].detail == "Add 7 and 8"
assert changed.events[2].detail == "15"
assert changed.events[3].detail == "15"
The tool choice stays add; the task, observation, and answer change. Now test a sum of zero. Zero is a valid result, not a missing observation.
zero = run_agent(Task(-5, 5))
assert zero.status == "complete"
assert zero.answer == 0

title: Run the Offline Agent Smoke Lab
section: 4. Let the tool succeed but stop the run
text:
4. Let the tool succeed but stop the run
What changes when the runtime permits only one decision?
limited = run_agent(Task(7, 5), max_steps=1)
assert limited.status == "budget_exhausted"
assert limited.answer is None
assert [event.kind for event in limited.events] == [
    "task", "tool_call", "observation", "budget_exhausted"
]
The first decision requests the tool. The addition succeeds, but the runtime does not permit a second decision to return a final answer. The result is intentionally incomplete. Asking the model to stop is different from enforcing a limit in code.


Hint: find the boundary that consumes the budget

max_steps counts calls to the model’s decide method, not events. With a budget of two, the fake model first requests addition and then returns its observation. Increase the budget back to two and verify that the final answer reappears.

title: Run the Offline Agent Smoke Lab
text:
5. Request an unavailable capability
This test double requests a shell tool. Predict whether any command can run.
from freecampus_agents.lab import Decision


class UnavailableToolModel:
    def decide(self, task, observation):
        return Decision("tool", tool="shell")


denied = run_agent(Task(7, 5), model=UnavailableToolModel())
assert denied.status == "denied"
assert denied.answer is None
assert [event.kind for event in denied.events] == ["task", "denied"]
A requested tool name is not permission. The runtime has no shell implementation and returns denied. It also rejects final answers that lack a preceding observation or disagree with it. Unexpected exceptions from a custom model propagate to the caller; this small scaffold does not promise production error recovery.

Restart and run the notebook from the top. Save the ordinary, zero-sum, limited, and denied cases. Record your Python version, package version, commands, predicted results, and actual statuses in an engineering journal.

1. Write Tool Contracts Models Can Use
Design names, descriptions, schemas, examples, preconditions, and postconditions that separate model-facing affordances from implementation details. Measure ambiguous tool selection and distinguish discovering a tool from permission to execute it.


2. Normalize Errors, Timeouts, and Cancellation
Create a tool-result envelope distinguishing invalid input, denied action, transient failure, permanent failure, partial result, timeout, and cancellation. Prevent raw stack traces or secrets from entering model context.


3. Make Retries and Side Effects Safe
Separate queries from commands; introduce idempotency keys, deduplication, retry policies, and compensation. Diagnose a duplicate-charge scenario caused by naive retry.


4. Enforce Least Privilege and Approval
Scope credentials and tools by task, resource, action, and time. Add policy checks and human confirmation for high-impact, irreversible, or externally visible operations.

title: Check Your Python Readiness
section: 1. Separate returning a result from displaying it
text:
1. Separate returning a result from displaying it
Before running, predict which call returns data to its caller.
def display_total(left, right):
    print(left + right)


def add(left, right):
    return left + right


shown = display_total(2, 3)
returned = add(2, 3)
assert shown is None
assert returned == 5
The first function displays 5, then returns None implicitly. The second returns an integer without displaying it. A tool consumer needs data it can inspect, not just a message printed to a terminal. Change the two inputs and update the independent expected value before running again.

title: Check Your Python Readiness
text:
2. Track shared mutable state
Predict the final list before running. Does assigning a second name copy the list?
events = ["task"]
shared = events
shared.append("tool_call")
assert events == ["task", "tool_call"]
Both names refer to the same list. Replace shared = events with shared = events.copy(). Now events should remain ["task"]; change the assertion to reflect the intended contract. Explain why hidden sharing could corrupt a trace.

title: Check Your Python Readiness
section: 3. Locate the failure before changing the expected value
text:
3. Locate the failure before changing the expected value
Predict the exception produced by the conversion, then inspect its exact message.
try:
    value = int("twelve")
except ValueError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__, str(error))
Python raises ValueError because this text does not represent an integer. Handling it does not create a valid answer. A real caller needs a policy such as rejecting input, asking for clarification, or reporting failure.

title: Contribute a Reproducible Learning Lab
section: 3. Author the lesson, not just its summary
text:
3. Author the lesson, not just its summary
Include a concrete task, 3–5 opening questions, a measurable outcome, active-time estimate, explanations, predictions, controlled changes, and debugging practice. Use three small checkpoints for concept, evidence, and failure diagnosis; give plausible distractors and explanations. Finish with a checked lab and primary references. Overviews stay quiz-free; planned project outlines are not assessments.
Unit challenges take 90–180 minutes and include a contract, progressive checks, three hint levels, injected failures, a hidden solution, and an evidence record. The templates are scaffolds outside the rendered course, not publishable lessons.

title: Contribute a Reproducible Learning Lab
text:
4. Keep publication records synchronized
When a lesson is genuinely available, update its catalog status, front matter, course progress IDs, available counts, outcome map, and sidebar together. Add the Colab include and a unique notebook path. Never link a planned path that does not exist. Do not enable whole-course completion until the completion contract is ready.

title: Contribute a Reproducible Learning Lab
text:
5. Check from a clean environment
Use Poetry 2.4+ within the 2.x series. A tracked poetry.lock now exists; validate it against pyproject.toml with poetry check --lock --strict before installation. If they disagree, review and regenerate the lock through the dependency-maintenance workflow, not by hand or by borrowing another course’s lock. Explicit CI lock enforcement and clean supported-platform installation evidence remain release work. A passing metadata check alone does not establish a fully reproducible release.
Conda + Poetry are required locally and in CI. conda.yaml supplies Python 3.12, Poetry, Node.js, and pip. Poetry installs project dependencies directly into the activated Conda environment. The shared poetry.toml disables separate virtual environments; the environment check rejects nested venvs or mismatched tools. Use poetry install, not synchronization, to preserve Conda-owned tooling. Activate the environment in each terminal and select its Python in your editor. Pre-commit hooks use these installed tools rather than creating hook environments.
conda env create -f conda.yaml  # First setup only
conda activate fc-agentic
python scripts/check_environment.py
poetry check --lock --strict
poetry install --all-extras --with docs
python scripts/check_environment.py
poetry run pytest -q
poetry run ruff check src tests scripts
poetry run ruff format --check src tests scripts
poetry run mypy src
poetry build
poetry run makim docs.build
git diff --check
poetry run makim clean.tmp
The build renders HTML, exports notebooks, and verifies expected output files. Open at least one desktop and narrow-screen quiz when browser tooling is available. Restart the smoke notebook and run from the top. Report skipped checks and external limitations rather than treating unrun checks as passing.

title: Contribute a Reproducible Learning Lab
text:
6. Keep current-system examples reproducible
Teach the transferable mechanism in the small course runtime first. The tracked docs/courses/agentic-ai-engineering/_technology.yml is a research register, not an installed dependency list or additional lesson catalog. It records the owning lesson IDs, accountable maintainer, primary sources, documentation review date, next review, known specification revision, and integration-validation state. Its initial entries are not validated integrations: no tested product version or execution evidence is implied by a documentation review.
Recheck each entry at least every 90 days and before authoring or publication. Review immediately after a relevant security advisory, breaking change, deprecation, or license/provider-policy change. CI checks register structure and lesson ownership offline; it cannot verify that a human reviewed a source or that an upstream service is still compatible.
Before supporting a live integration, record its exact release/commit, SDK and protocol revision, model revision, effective configuration, operating system, execution boundary, resource budget, and licensed fixture provenance. Preserve ordinary, denied-action, and held-out results plus independent review and an exit/rollback path. Set a validated version only when those artifacts exist. Do not use a floating latest or a vendor benchmark as execution evidence. Withhold or replace integrations whose maintenance or safety assumptions fail.

Use the case study appropriate to the engineering question

Skills: teach instruction packaging, selective loading, provenance, and review separately from tool authorization. The Agent Skills specification documents the format; host support for experimental permission metadata can differ.
OpenClaw: use architecture/configuration inspection for persistent assistants, then optional isolated operational experiments after Units 15–16. Its documentation states that sandboxing is off by default and that one gateway assumes a trusted boundary, not hostile multi-tenancy. Sandboxing and security guidance.
Hermes Agent by Nous Research: study the distinction between factual memory and reusable procedures, then compare no skill, a reviewed skill, and a generated skill on held-out tasks. Changing a skill is not training model weights or proof of improvement. Skills documentation.
Serving engines: verify a maintained vLLM or SGLang release for a new lab; retain TGI as a legacy/migration comparison following the upstream maintenance notice.

These source observations were reviewed on 2026-09-19; reverify before use. Early lessons use synthetic documents and sanitized architecture examples, not live assistants. Actual product execution is optional after the safety units, inside a disposable verified boundary with restricted mounts/egress, reviewed skills, synthetic identities, resource limits, and approvals. Do not require personal accounts, credentials, unattended host access, or paid services.
Every lab distinguishes course fixture execution, analysis of recorded observations, and optional live integration. A Colab replay is a useful free learning route but cannot establish OS containment, real-model learning gains, deployment reliability, or hardware performance. Keep the evaluator and held-out answers outside the agent’s writable boundary. Use observable actions and concise external rationales, never private chain-of-thought.
Substitute focused cases rather than silently enlarging lesson workloads. The published effort range is provisional: pilot the active work and account for milestone refinements, reviews, and optional setup separately.
Use the repository contribution guidance and Poetry’s basic usage for further detail.

Do I need to know Python?
Yes: project-ready Python or equivalent readiness. Check functions, collections, modules, exceptions, virtual environments, and tests in the readiness guide. This course does not re-teach beginner Python as an agent curriculum.

title: Course FAQ
section: Must I buy API credits or have a GPU?
text:
Must I buy API credits or have a GPU?
No paid service is required for the core route. The current smoke lab uses a standard-library fake model, without inference or network calls. Later lessons will provide deterministic fixtures alongside documented open-model/free execution paths. Optional provider comparisons must disclose costs and keep keys out of artifacts.

title: Course FAQ
text:
How do the notebooks work?
The website’s QMD pages are canonical. The build exports notebook copies to the published site; Colab links work after that branch is deployed. Overview notebooks contain orientation only. The smoke notebook bundles the small course package so its Python examples can execute offline without installing a package from a registry.

title: Course FAQ
text:
Is browser completion a qualification?
No. It is a local convenience, not verified assessment, identity, or certification. It does not sync between devices and can disappear when storage is cleared. Completion controls remain disabled for planned material. No certificate is offered.

title: Course FAQ
section: Where should I report a problem?
text:
Where should I report a problem?
Use the repository issue tracker. Include the page, environment, smallest reproduction, expected and actual behavior, and a redacted trace. Never include provider keys, personal data, or private prompts.
